claim: Mutations in the human N-glycanase 1 (NGLY1) cause a rare, multisystem congenital disorder with global developmental delay.
source: Mutations in the human N-glycanase 1 (NGLY1) cause a rare, multisystem congenital disorder with global developmental delay.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on NGLY1 deficiency.

claim: Drosophila Pngl encodes an N-glycanase.
source: Here we show that Drosophila Pngl encodes an N-glycanase and exhibits a high degree of functional conservation with human NGLY1.
evidence: This is supported by RTL spotting assays and cycloheximide decay assays showing deglycosylation activity.

claim: Drosophila Pngl exhibits a high degree of functional conservation with human NGLY1.
source: Here we show that Drosophila Pngl encodes an N-glycanase and exhibits a high degree of functional conservation with human NGLY1.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments showing that human NGLY1 can rescue Pngl mutant phenotypes.

claim: Loss of Pngl results in developmental midgut defects reminiscent of midgut-specific loss of BMP signaling.
source: Loss of Pngl results in developmental midgut defects reminiscent of midgut-specific loss of BMP signaling.
evidence: This is supported by observations of shortened gastric caeca and loss of acid zone in Pngl mutants.

claim: Pngl mutant larvae exhibit a severe midgut clearance defect.
source: Pngl mutant larvae also exhibit a severe midgut clearance defect, which cannot be fully explained by impaired BMP signaling.
evidence: This is supported by bromophenol blue feeding assays showing food accumulation in Pngl mutants.

claim: The midgut clearance defect in Pngl mutants cannot be fully explained by impaired BMP signaling.
source: Pngl mutant larvae also exhibit a severe midgut clearance defect, which cannot be fully explained by impaired BMP signaling.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of Pngl and dpp knockdown phenotypes showing differential effects on food accumulation.

claim: Pngl is primarily required in the mesoderm during Drosophila development.
source: Genetic experiments indicate that Pngl is primarily required in the mesoderm during Drosophila development.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi knockdown and rescue experiments using mesodermal and endodermal drivers.

claim: Loss of Pngl results in a severe decrease in the level of Dpp homodimers.
source: Loss of Pngl results in a severe decrease in the level of Dpp homodimers and abolishes BMP autoregulation in the visceral mesoderm mediated by Dpp and Tkv homodimers.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot analysis showing decreased Dpp dimer bands in Pngl mutants.

claim: Loss of Pngl abolishes BMP autoregulation in the visceral mesoderm mediated by Dpp and Tkv homodimers.
source: Loss of Pngl results in a severe decrease in the level of Dpp homodimers and abolishes BMP autoregulation in the visceral mesoderm mediated by Dpp and Tkv homodimers.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining showing lack of pMad in dpp-lacZ expressing cells in Pngl mutants.

claim: NGLY1 encodes an evolutionarily conserved enzyme that catalyzes the cleavage of N-glycans from glycoproteins.
source: NGLY1 (N-glycanase 1) encodes an evolutionarily conserved enzyme that catalyzes the cleavage of N-glycans from glycoproteins (Suzuki et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: NGLY1 mutations have been identified in patients with an autosomal recessive developmental disorder called NGLY1 deficiency.
source: Whole-genome and -exome sequencing has recently resulted in the identification of NGLY1 mutations in patients with an autosomal recessive developmental disorder called NGLY1 deficiency (Caglayan et al., 2015; Enns et al., 2014; Heeley and Shinawi, 2015; Need et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: NGLY1-deficient patients show global developmental delay, movement disorder, hypotonia, absent tears, peripheral neuropathy, constipation, and small feet and hands.
source: NGLY1-deficient patients show a host of phenotypes including global developmental delay, movement disorder, hypotonia, absent tears, peripheral neuropathy, constipation, and small feet and hands (Enns et al., 2014; Lam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The mechanism by which NGLY1 deficiency causes clinical phenotypes is not known.
source: The mechanism by which NGLY1 deficiency causes the above-mentioned clinical phenotypes is not known, and neither has NGLY1 been linked to any major developmental signaling pathway.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: NGLY1 has not been linked to any major developmental signaling pathway.
source: The mechanism by which NGLY1 deficiency causes the above-mentioned clinical phenotypes is not known, and neither has NGLY1 been linked to any major developmental signaling pathway.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: In yeast, N-glycanase 1 has been associated with endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (ERAD).
source: In yeast, N-glycanase 1 (Peptide: N-glycanase or PNGase, encoded by PNG1) has been associated with endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (ERAD) (Suzuki, 2007; Suzuki et al., 2016), a process that plays a crucial role in the proteasome-mediated degradation of misfolded proteins (Brodsky, 2012; Smith et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Null mutants for yeast PNG1 do not show apparent phenotypic abnormalities and exhibit normal growth rate and viability under a variety of experimental conditions.
source: However, null mutants for yeast PNG1 do not show apparent phenotypic abnormalities and exhibit normal growth rate and viability under a variety of experimental conditions (Suzuki et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In C. elegans, SKN-1 needs to be retrotranslocated from ER to cytoplasm by ERAD machinery and deglycosylated by NGLY1 to function properly.
source: A recent study has provided strong evidence that in C. elegans, a transcription factor called SKN-1 (homolog to mammalian NFE2L1/2) needs to be retrotranslocated from ER to cytoplasm by ERAD machinery and deglycosylated by NGLY1 (PNG-1 in worms) to function properly (Lehrbach and Ruvkun, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Deglycosylation of SKN-1 does not result in its degradation, but instead promotes its activation.
source: However, deglycosylation does not result in SKN-1 degradation, but instead promotes the activation of SKN-1 so that it can mediate the necessary transcriptional response to proteasome disruption (Lehrbach and Ruvkun, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Mouse embryonic fibroblasts lacking NGLY1 did not show impairment and/or delay in the degradation of misfolded proteins.
source: Moreover, mouse embryonic fibroblasts lacking NGLY1 did not show impairment and/or delay in the degradation of misfolded proteins, but displayed an unconventional deglycosylation reaction that may generate aggregation-prone proteins harboring N-GlcNAc and result in cell toxicity in the absence of NGLY1 (Huang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: NGLY1 does not seem to directly promote the degradation of misfolded proteins in animals.
source: Therefore, although NGLY1 seems to be functionally associated with the ERAD machinery, it does not seem to directly promote the degradation of misfolded proteins in animals.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited studies showing lack of degradation defects in NGLY1-deficient cells.

claim: Loss-of-function mutants of Drosophila Pngl result in semi-lethality and sterility.
source: Human NGLY1 has a single Drosophila homolog called PNGase-like (Pngl), whose loss-of-function mutants result in semi-lethality and sterility (Funakoshi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Ubiquitous expression of wild-type human NGLY1 rescues the homozygous lethality of Pngl mutants.
source: Ubiquitous expression of WT human NGLY1, but not NGLY1-ΔR402, was able to rescue the lethality in both Pngl alleles (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by eclosion test data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: NGLY1-ΔR402 does not rescue the homozygous lethality of Pngl mutants.
source: Ubiquitous expression of WT human NGLY1, but not NGLY1-ΔR402, was able to rescue the lethality in both Pngl alleles (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by eclosion test data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Pngl mutant escaper flies are sterile and short-lived.
source: Both male and female Pngl–/– escaper flies are sterile and short-lived (Figure 1C and D) (Funakoshi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by fertility and longevity test data shown in Figures 1C and 1D, and citation to published literature.

claim: Adult Pngl mutant flies rescued by NGLY1-WT do not show sterility and short lifespan phenotypes.
source: However, adult Pngl–/–; Act > NGLY1 WT animals do not show these phenotypes (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by fertility and longevity test data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: Drosophila Pngl can suppress the growth of png1Δ yeast cells in media without leucine to the same extent as yeast Png1.
source: An HA-tagged version of the fly Pngl suppressed the growth of the yeast cell in media without leucine to the same extent as the Sc-Png1 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by RTL spotting assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Pngl harboring a C303A mutation in its putative catalytic domain fails to rescue PNGase function in yeast.
source: Meanwhile, Pngl harboring a C303A mutation in its putative catalytic domain (Pngl-HA-C303A) failed to rescue PNGase function (Figure 1E), even though WT and C303A versions are expressed at comparable levels (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by RTL spotting assay and Western blot data shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: Drosophila Pngl is able to deglycosylate RTL and facilitate the efficient degradation of the RTL protein.
source: These observations strongly suggest that Drosophila Pngl is able to deglycosylate RTL and facilitate the efficient degradation of the RTL protein.
evidence: This is inferred from RTL spotting assay results showing growth suppression in leucine-deficient media.

claim: Expression of yeast Png1 or fly Pngl increases the relative level of the deglycosylated form of RTAΔ in a time-dependent manner.
source: Expression of Sc-Png1 or fly Pngl increased the relative level of the deglycosylated form (g0) in a time-dependent manner (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is supported by cycloheximide decay assay data shown in Figures 1G and 1H.

claim: Pngl-C303A fails to remove glycans from RTAΔ.
source: However, Pngl-C303A failed to remove glycans from RTAΔ.
evidence: This is supported by cycloheximide decay assay data showing no increase in deglycosylated form.

claim: Human NGLY1 can compensate for the lack of yeast Png1 in the RTL assay.
source: Similar experiments indicate that human NGLY1, but not the C309A catalytic mutant NGLY1, can also compensate for the lack of Sc-Png1 in the RTL assay (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by RTL spotting assay data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The C309A catalytic mutant of human NGLY1 cannot compensate for the lack of yeast Png1 in the RTL assay.
source: Similar experiments indicate that human NGLY1, but not the C309A catalytic mutant NGLY1, can also compensate for the lack of Sc-Png1 in the RTL assay (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by RTL spotting assay data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: NGLY1-ΔR402 shows a weak rescue of PNGase activity in the RTL assay, suggesting it is a hypomorphic allele.
source: Of note, NGLY1-ΔR402 showed a weak rescue of the PNGase activity in this assay, suggesting that it is a hypomorphic allele.
evidence: This is inferred from RTL spotting assay data showing partial growth suppression.

claim: Drosophila Pngl is an N-glycanase enzyme.
source: Altogether, these observations indicate that Drosophila Pngl is indeed an N-glycanase enzyme and that there is high level of functional conservation between Pngl and its yeast and human homologs.
evidence: This is supported by multiple functional assays showing deglycosylation activity.

claim: There is a high level of functional conservation between Pngl and its yeast and human homologs.
source: Altogether, these observations indicate that Drosophila Pngl is indeed an N-glycanase enzyme and that there is high level of functional conservation between Pngl and its yeast and human homologs.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments and functional assays across species.

claim: Control larvae harbor four finger-like structures called gastric caeca in the anterior part of the midgut.
source: In the anterior part of the midgut, control larvae harbor four finger-like structures called gastric caeca (Figure 2A and B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which play key roles in the insect digestive system, including water and ion transport and secretion of enzymes (Pullikuth et al., 2006; Volkmann and Peters, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by images in Figure 2A and 2B, and citations to published literature.

claim: Gastric caeca play key roles in the insect digestive system, including water and ion transport and secretion of enzymes.
source: In the anterior part of the midgut, control larvae harbor four finger-like structures called gastric caeca (Figure 2A and B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which play key roles in the insect digestive system, including water and ion transport and secretion of enzymes (Pullikuth et al., 2006; Volkmann and Peters, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Pngl mutant larvae show a severe shortening of the gastric caeca.
source: Pngl–/– larvae showed a severe shortening of the gastric caeca (Figure 2C, red asterisks) compared to y w and heterozygote controls (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by images in Figure 2C showing shortened gastric caeca.

claim: Control larvae harbor a specific region in the middle midgut called the 'acid zone', which has a luminal pH of less than 2.3.
source: Control larvae harbor a specific region in the middle midgut called the 'acid zone', which has a luminal pH of less than 2.3 and is considered the fly stomach (Figure 2A) (Dubreuil, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by schematic in Figure 2A and citation to published literature.

claim: The acid zone is considered the fly stomach.
source: Control larvae harbor a specific region in the middle midgut called the 'acid zone', which has a luminal pH of less than 2.3 and is considered the fly stomach (Figure 2A) (Dubreuil, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Pngl mutant larvae are almost completely devoid of the yellow color in the midgut, indicating a loss of acid zone.
source: Pngl–/– larvae are almost completely devoid of the yellow color in the midgut, indicating a loss of acid zone (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by bromophenol blue staining images in Figure 2E.

claim: Pnglex18/ex18 and Pnglex20/ex20 animals show shortened gastric caeca and a loss of acid zone.
source: Similar to Pnglex14/ex14 larvae, Pnglex18/ex18 and Pnglex20/ex20 animals showed shortened gastric caeca and a loss of acid zone (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and not shown).
evidence: This is supported by images in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pnglex14 and Pnglex18 hemizygous animals show semi-lethality and midgut phenotypes.
source: Moreover, Pnglex14 and Pnglex18 hemizygous animals (over a deficiency allele) showed semi-lethality and midgut phenotypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and not shown), suggesting that ex14 and ex18 deletions are genetic null alleles.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: ex14 and ex18 deletions are genetic null alleles.
source: Moreover, Pnglex14 and Pnglex18 hemizygous animals (over a deficiency allele) showed semi-lethality and midgut phenotypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and not shown), suggesting that ex14 and ex18 deletions are genetic null alleles.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that hemizygous animals show the same phenotypes as homozygous mutants.

claim: Loss of Pngl leads to specific midgut defects in Drosophila larvae.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that loss of Pngl leads to specific midgut defects in Drosophila larvae.
evidence: This is supported by observations of gastric caeca shortening and acid zone loss.

claim: In Drosophila embryos, Dpp signals from visceral mesoderm to endoderm and is required for midgut specification.
source: In Drosophila embryos, a member of the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) family called Decapentaplegic (Dpp) signals from VM to endoderm and is required for midgut specification (Dubreuil, 2004; Panganiban et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: BMP signaling from visceral mesoderm in PS3 and PS7 is transduced by phosphorylated Mad (pMad) in midgut endoderm.
source: Specifically, BMP signaling from VM in parasegment 3 (PS3) and PS7 is transduced by phosphorylated Mothers against dpp (pMad) (Newfeld et al., 1996) in midgut endoderm, resulting in the formation of the gastric caeca and the acid zone, respectively (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by schematic in Figure 2F and citation to published literature.

claim: BMP signaling from VM in PS3 and PS7 results in the formation of the gastric caeca and the acid zone, respectively.
source: Specifically, BMP signaling from VM in parasegment 3 (PS3) and PS7 is transduced by phosphorylated Mothers against dpp (pMad) (Newfeld et al., 1996) in midgut endoderm, resulting in the formation of the gastric caeca and the acid zone, respectively (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature and schematic representation.

claim: Pngl mutant embryos show a dramatic decrease in the level of pMad in PS3 and PS7.
source: However, Pngl–/– embryos showed a dramatic decrease in the level of pMad in PS3 and PS7 (Figure 2H and H').
evidence: This is supported by pMad immunostaining images in Figure 2H and H'.

claim: Loss of BMP signaling in PS7 results in lack of second midgut constriction.
source: Loss of BMP signaling in PS7 results in lack of second midgut constriction and impairs the expression of the acid-secreting (copper) cell-specific homeodomain gene labial in PS7 endodermal cells (Immerglück et al., 1990; Nellen et al., 1994; Panganiban et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Loss of BMP signaling in PS7 impairs the expression of labial in PS7 endodermal cells.
source: Loss of BMP signaling in PS7 results in lack of second midgut constriction and impairs the expression of the acid-secreting (copper) cell-specific homeodomain gene labial in PS7 endodermal cells (Immerglück et al., 1990; Nellen et al., 1994; Panganiban et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Stage 15 Pngl mutant embryos show no Labial signal in the PS7 region.
source: However, in stage 15 Pngl–/– embryos, no Labial signal was detectable in the PS7 region (Figure 2J and J').
evidence: This is supported by Labial immunostaining images in Figure 2J and J'.

claim: Stage 16 Pngl mutant embryos lack Labial staining and second constriction.
source: However, stage 16 Pngl–/– embryos lack Labial staining and second constriction (Figure 2L and L'), in agreement with impaired BMP signaling in PS7.
evidence: This is supported by Labial and Fas3 immunostaining images in Figure 2L and L'.

claim: Pngl is required for mesoderm-to-endoderm BMP signaling in Drosophila embryos.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that Pngl is required for mesoderm-to-endoderm BMP signaling in Drosophila embryos.
evidence: This is supported by pMad and Labial staining data showing impaired BMP signaling in Pngl mutants.

claim: Pngl knockdown with Mef2-GAL4 results in 100% lethality at room temperature.
source: When crossed to the mesodermal driver Mef2-GAL4, the PnglRNAi KK101641 strain (http://stockcenter.vdrc.at/control/main) resulted in 100% lethality at room temperature and recapitulated the gastric caeca shortening and acid zone loss phenotypes observed in Pngl mutants (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is supported by eclosion test data in Figure 3A and phenotypic images in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: Pngl knockdown with Mef2-GAL4 recapitulates the gastric caeca shortening and acid zone loss phenotypes observed in Pngl mutants.
source: When crossed to the mesodermal driver Mef2-GAL4, the PnglRNAi KK101641 strain (http://stockcenter.vdrc.at/control/main) resulted in 100% lethality at room temperature and recapitulated the gastric caeca shortening and acid zone loss phenotypes observed in Pngl mutants (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic images in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: Pngl knockdown with how24B-GAL4 results in partial lethality and acid zone defects in larvae.
source: In addition, Pngl KD by another mesodermal driver called how24B-GAL4 resulted in partial lethality and acid zone defects in larvae (Figure 3A and E).
evidence: This is supported by eclosion test data in Figure 3A and phenotypic images in Figure 3E.

claim: Pngl knockdown with how24B-GAL4 does not affect gastric caeca formation.
source: Pngl KD with how24B-GAL4 did not affect gastric caeca formation (Figure 3D), likely because this driver induces transgene expression later than Mef2-GAL4 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), after gastric caeca anlagen have already been formed.
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic images in Figure 3D and expression pattern data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: how24B-GAL4 induces transgene expression later than Mef2-GAL4.
source: Pngl KD with how24B-GAL4 did not affect gastric caeca formation (Figure 3D), likely because this driver induces transgene expression later than Mef2-GAL4 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), after gastric caeca anlagen have already been formed.
evidence: This is supported by expression pattern data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pngl knockdown by two endodermal drivers does not result in lethality and gut phenotypes.
source: However, Pngl KD by two endodermal drivers did not result in lethality and gut phenotypes (Figure 3A and F–I).
evidence: This is supported by eclosion test data in Figure 3A and phenotypic images in Figures 3F-I.

claim: Overexpression of human NGLY1 with Mef2-GAL4 and how24B-GAL4 rescues the lethality of Pngl alleles.
source: Moreover, overexpression of human NGLY1 with Mef2-GAL4 and how24B-GAL4 rescued the lethality of the Pngl alleles (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by eclosion test data in Figure 3J.

claim: Mef2-GAL4 rescues the lethality of Pngl mutants more efficiently than how24B-GAL4.
source: In agreement with the severity of their corresponding KD phenotypes and expression patterns, Mef2-GAL4 rescued the lethality more efficiently than how24B-GAL4 (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by eclosion test data in Figure 3J.

claim: During Drosophila development, Pngl is primarily required in the mesoderm to ensure animal survival and to promote BMP signaling from visceral mesoderm to endoderm.
source: Together, these data indicate that during Drosophila development Pngl is primarily required in the mesoderm to ensure animal survival and to promote BMP signaling from visceral mesoderm to endoderm.
evidence: This is supported by tissue-specific knockdown and rescue experiments.

claim: Overexpression of wild-type Pngl rescues gastric caeca and acid zone defects of Pngl mutants.
source: As shown in Figure 3K and L, overexpression of wild-type Pngl rescues gastric caeca and acid zone defects of Pngl mutants.
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic images in Figures 3K and 3L.

claim: Overexpression of Pngl-C303A fails to rescue Pngl midgut phenotypes.
source: However, the mutant version fails to rescue Pngl midgut phenotypes (Figure 3M and N), even though Western blot shows that this mutation does not affect the expression level or stability of Pngl (Figure 3O).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic images in Figures 3M and 3N, and Western blot data in Figure 3O.

claim: The C303A mutation does not affect the expression level or stability of Pngl.
source: However, the mutant version fails to rescue Pngl midgut phenotypes (Figure 3M and N), even though Western blot shows that this mutation does not affect the expression level or stability of Pngl (Figure 3O).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 3O.

claim: The BMP signaling impairment observed in Pngl larval midguts is due to the lack of Pngl's enzymatic activity.
source: Together, these data indicate that the BMP signaling impairment observed in Pngl larval midguts is due to the lack of Pngl's enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the failure of catalytically inactive Pngl to rescue midgut phenotypes.

claim: In the absence of midgut acidification, larvae are able to reach adulthood.
source: Previous reports indicate that in the absence of midgut acidification, larvae are able to reach adulthood (Dubreuil et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Regulatory mutations that result in specific loss of dpp expression in PS3 and a complete loss of gastric caeca only show a partial lethality.
source: Moreover, regulatory mutations that result in specific loss of dpp expression in PS3 and a complete loss of gastric caeca only show a partial lethality (Masucci and Hoffmann, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Impaired Dpp signaling in the midgut is not sufficient to fully explain the lethality of Pngl mutants.
source: Accordingly, impaired Dpp signaling in the midgut is not sufficient to fully explain the lethality of Pngl mutants, especially given that gastric caeca are not completely lost.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with dpp knockdown phenotypes and published literature.

claim: Animals undergoing dpp knockdown by mesodermal drivers show a higher survival compared to those undergoing Pngl knockdown.
source: Indeed, animals undergoing dpp KD by the same mesodermal drivers showed a higher survival compared to those undergoing Pngl KD (Figure 3P, compare to 3A).
evidence: This is supported by eclosion test data in Figures 3P and 3A.

claim: Mef2 > dppRNAi larvae exhibit a complete loss of gastric caeca and acid zone.
source: The weaker effects of dppRNAi are not likely to result from inefficient dpp KD, as Mef2 > dppRNAi larvae exhibited a complete loss of gastric caeca and acid zone, and how24B > dppRNAi larvae lost the acid zone but not the gastric caeca, suggesting a loss or severe impairment of mesoderm-to-endoderm BMP signaling corresponding to the spatiotemporal expression pattern of each driver (Figure 3Q–T).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic images in Figures 3Q-T.

claim: how24B > dppRNAi larvae lose the acid zone but not the gastric caeca.
source: The weaker effects of dppRNAi are not likely to result from inefficient dpp KD, as Mef2 > dppRNAi larvae exhibited a complete loss of gastric caeca and acid zone, and how24B > dppRNAi larvae lost the acid zone but not the gastric caeca, suggesting a loss or severe impairment of mesoderm-to-endoderm BMP signaling corresponding to the spatiotemporal expression pattern of each driver (Figure 3Q–T).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic images in Figures 3Q-T.

claim: Impaired Dpp signaling in the midgut can only partially account for the lethality observed in Pngl mutants.
source: These observations indicate that impaired Dpp signaling in the midgut can only partially account for the lethality observed in Pngl mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of survival rates between Pngl and dpp knockdown animals.

claim: Pngl also plays a Dpp-independent role in the mesoderm during Drosophila development.
source: So far our data suggest that Pngl also plays a Dpp-independent role in the mesoderm during Drosophila development.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Pngl knockdown causes more severe lethality than dpp knockdown.

claim: During the wandering phase, Pngl mutant larvae fail to empty their guts.
source: We noticed that during the wandering phase, Pngl–/– larvae failed to empty their guts (Figure 4A and A').
evidence: This is supported by images in Figure 4A and A' showing food accumulation.

claim: Control larvae typically empty their gut in 6 hours and reach the pre-pupal stage.
source: Control y w and Pngl+/– larvae typically emptied their gut in 6 hours and reached the pre-pupal stage (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by gut clearance assay data in Figure 4C.

claim: Most Pngl mutant larvae show a blue gut throughout the wandering stage.
source: In contrast, most Pngl–/– larvae showed a blue gut throughout the wandering stage (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by gut clearance assay data in Figure 4C.

claim: Loss of Pngl causes an impairment of gut clearance at late L3 stage.
source: These data indicate that loss of Pngl causes an impairment of gut clearance at late L3 stage.
evidence: This is supported by gut clearance assay data showing food retention in Pngl mutants.

claim: Mef2 > dppRNAi larvae exhibit a food accumulation phenotype milder than that observed in Pngl mutant and Mef2 > PnglRNAi larvae.
source: BPB feeding assays showed that Mef2 > dppRNAi larvae exhibit a food accumulation phenotype milder than that observed in Pngl mutant and Mef2 > PnglRNAi larvae, and that how24B > dppRNAi larvae do not exhibit any food accumulation phenotype, in contrast to how24B > PnglRNAi animals (Figure 4D, compare to Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by gut clearance assay data in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: how24B > dppRNAi larvae do not exhibit any food accumulation phenotype.
source: BPB feeding assays showed that Mef2 > dppRNAi larvae exhibit a food accumulation phenotype milder than that observed in Pngl mutant and Mef2 > PnglRNAi larvae, and that how24B > dppRNAi larvae do not exhibit any food accumulation phenotype, in contrast to how24B > PnglRNAi animals (Figure 4D, compare to Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by gut clearance assay data in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: The food accumulation phenotype observed in Pngl mutants is at least in part independent of impaired BMP signaling.
source: These data indicate that the food accumulation phenotype observed in Pngl mutants is at least in part independent of impaired BMP signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of food accumulation phenotypes between Pngl and dpp knockdown animals.

claim: In wild-type and Pngl+/– embryos at stage 13, the Dpp protein is expressed in ectodermal bands, several regions in the anterior part of the embryo and two rather narrow groups of cells corresponding to PS3 and PS7.
source: In WT and Pngl+/– embryos at stage 13, the Dpp protein is expressed in ectodermal bands, several regions in the anterior part of the embryo and two rather narrow groups of cells corresponding to PS3 and PS7, where it shows a punctate pattern superimposed on a diffuse signal (Figure 5A, B, G and H).
evidence: This is supported by Dpp immunostaining images in Figures 5A, B, G, and H.

claim: In stage 13 Pngl mutant embryos, Dpp staining is somewhat weaker overall, but staining in PS3 and PS7 is observed, with a notable decrease in puncta.
source: Overall, the staining is somewhat weaker in Pngl–/– embryos, but staining in PS3 and PS7 is observed, with a notable decrease in puncta (Figure 5C and I).
evidence: This is supported by Dpp immunostaining images in Figures 5C and I.

claim: By stage 14, a broad and strong Dpp expression domain can be observed in PS3 and PS7 in control embryos.
source: By stage 14, a broad and strong Dpp expression domain can be observed in PS3 and PS7 in control embryos (Figure 5D, E, J and K).
evidence: This is supported by Dpp immunostaining images in Figures 5D, E, J, and K.

claim: In stage 14 Pngl mutant embryos, Dpp expression in the visceral mesoderm remains weak and narrow in PS3 and PS7.
source: In contrast, Dpp expression in the VM remains weak and narrow in PS3 and PS7 of mutant embryos (Figure 5F and L).
evidence: This is supported by Dpp immunostaining images in Figures 5F and L.

claim: The pattern of Dpp expression in the ectoderm is similar in control and Pngl mutant embryos at both stages 13 and 14.
source: Notably, the pattern of Dpp expression in the ectoderm is similar in control and Pngl–/– embryos at both stages, even though the staining seems to be slightly weaker in mutant embryos (Figure 5A–F).
evidence: This is supported by Dpp immunostaining images in Figures 5A-F.

claim: A failure to expand the Dpp expression domain in the visceral mesoderm leads to impaired mesoderm-to-endoderm BMP signaling in Pngl mutants.
source: These results suggest that a failure to expand the Dpp expression domain in the VM leads to impaired mesoderm-to-endoderm BMP signaling in Pngl mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from observations of narrow Dpp expression domain and decreased pMad in Pngl mutants.

claim: Embryos heterozygous for the dppS2 allele exhibit a decrease in Dpp expression at stage 13 in PS7, even compared to Pngl mutant embryos.
source: Embryos heterozygous for this allele exhibit a decrease in Dpp expression at stage 13 in PS7, even compared to Pngl–/– embryos (Figure 5M, compare to Figure 5G, H and I).
evidence: This is supported by Dpp immunostaining images in Figure 5M compared to Figures 5G, H, and I.

claim: dppS2/+ embryos show Dpp propagation at stage 14 and proper Dpp signaling from mesoderm to endoderm.
source: Nevertheless, these embryos show Dpp propagation at stage 14 and proper Dpp signaling from mesoderm to endoderm, as evidenced by analyzing the expression of Dpp targets in the embryonic midgut and gastric caeca and acid zone in larvae (Figure 5N and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Dpp immunostaining and phenotypic analysis in Figure 5N and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Decreased Dpp expression by itself cannot explain the impaired Dpp propagation and loss of mesoderm-to-endoderm BMP signaling in Pngl mutants.
source: These data suggest that decreased Dpp expression by itself cannot explain the impaired Dpp propagation and loss of mesoderm-to-endoderm BMP signaling in Pngl mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with dppS2/+ embryos that show lower Dpp expression but normal signaling.

claim: At stage 13, the majority of pMad staining is localized to the visceral mesoderm and only a few cells are stained in the endoderm.
source: At stage 13 the majority of pMad staining is localized to the VM and only a few cells are stained in the endoderm (Figure 5O and O').
evidence: This is supported by pMad immunostaining images in Figures 5O and O'.

claim: At stage 14, BMP signaling spreads through the endoderm and expands in PS7.
source: Later at stage 14, BMP signaling spreads through the endoderm and expands in PS7, as evidenced by the presence of many pMad-positive endodermal cells (Figure 5P and P'; GFP–, round nuclei).
evidence: This is supported by pMad immunostaining images in Figures 5P and P'.

claim: An autoregulatory Dpp para-autocrine loop exists in PS7, which acts through Ubx expression in visceral mesoderm and results in maintenance and accumulation of Dpp expression in visceral mesoderm cells.
source: These observations are in agreement with previous reports suggesting the existence of an autoregulatory Dpp para-autocrine loop in PS7, which acts through Ultrabithorax (Ubx) expression in VM and results in maintenance and accumulation of Dpp expression in VM cells (Figure 5Q) (Bienz, 1997; Hursh et al., 1993; Staehling-Hampton and Hoffmann, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and schematic in Figure 5Q.

claim: In Pngl+/– embryos at stage 13, a row of cells co-expressing pMad and βGAL (dpp-lacZ) is found in PS7.
source: In Pngl+/– embryos at stage 13, we found a row of cells co-expressing pMad and βGAL (Figure 5R–R'), suggesting para-autocrine activation.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images in Figures 5R-R'.

claim: In PS7 of Pngl mutant embryos at stage 13, dpp-lacZ expression can be detected, but pMad staining is absent.
source: In PS7 of Pngl–/– embryos at stage 13, dpp-lacZ expression can be detected, but pMad staining is absent (Figure 5S–S').
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images in Figures 5S-S'.

claim: In Pngl mutant PS7, the initial, Ubx-dependent dpp expression occurs, but the autoactivation loop is impaired.
source: These results indicate that in Pngl–/– PS7, the initial, Ubx-dependent dpp expression (Sun et al., 1995) occurs, but the autoactivation loop is impaired.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of dpp-lacZ expression but absence of pMad in Pngl mutant PS7.

claim: At stage 14, the Dpp expression domain expands in Pngl+/– embryos and dpp-lacZ expressing cells can be seen in multiple layers.
source: At stage 14, the Dpp expression domain expands in Pngl+/– embryos and dpp-lacZ expressing cells can be seen in multiple layers.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining observations.

claim: Most if not all dpp-lacZ expressing cells in stage 14 Pngl+/– embryos co-express pMad, likely due to autoactivation.
source: Most if not all dpp-lacZ expressing cells still co-express pMad, likely due to autoactivation, while endodermal cells, as receiving cells, only express pMad (Figure 5T–T').
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images in Figures 5T-T' and inference about autoactivation.

claim: In stage 14 Pngl mutant embryos, dpp-lacZ-expressing cells remain confined to their initial narrow domain in PS7, and pMad staining is still not detectable.
source: In stage 14 Pngl–/– embryos, dpp-lacZ-expressing cells remain confined to their initial narrow domain in PS7, and pMad staining is still not detectable (Figure 5U–U').
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images in Figures 5U-U'.

claim: The dorsal ectodermal region shows a comparable expression pattern and intensity in the dorsal ectodermal bands of Pngl+/– and Pngl mutant embryos for both dpp-lacZ and pMad.
source: This is in contrast to the dorsal ectodermal region, which showed a comparable expression pattern and intensity in the dorsal ectodermal bands of Pngl+/– and Pngl–/– embryos for both dpp-lacZ and pMad (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pngl is not required for the initial expression of dpp through Ubx in Drosophila embryos but is required for the autoregulatory role of Dpp in the visceral mesoderm.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that Pngl is not required for the initial expression of dpp through Ubx in Drosophila embryos but is required for the autoregulatory role of Dpp in the VM.
evidence: This is supported by observations of dpp-lacZ expression without pMad in Pngl mutants.

claim: In control animals, dpp-GFP overexpression by Mef2-GAL4 results in broad pMad staining in embryonic midgut and ectopic pMad expression throughout the ectoderm.
source: In control animals, dpp-GFP overexpression by Mef2-GAL4 resulted in broad pMad staining in embryonic midgut and ectopic pMad expression throughout the ectoderm (Figure 6A and D).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images in Figures 6A and D.

claim: In Pngl mutant embryos, mesodermal expression of Dpp-GFP restores pMad expression in PS3 and PS7.
source: In Pngl–/– embryos, mesodermal expression of Dpp-GFP restored pMad expression in PS3 and PS7, indicating a rescue of BMP signaling from VM to endoderm (Figure 6B and E, compare to Figure 6C and F).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images in Figures 6B and E compared to Figures 6C and F.

claim: In Pngl mutant embryos with mesodermal Dpp-GFP expression, pMad staining is limited to PS3 and PS7, and ectopic pMad expression in the ectoderm is almost completely suppressed.
source: Notably, in Pngl–/–; Mef2 > dpp GFP embryos, pMad staining was limited to PS3 and PS7, and ectopic pMad expression in the ectoderm was almost completely suppressed (Figure 6B and E), indicating that loss of Pngl dramatically decreases the ability of mesodermally-expressed Dpp-GFP to induce ectopic BMP signaling.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images in Figures 6B and E.

claim: Loss of Pngl dramatically decreases the ability of mesodermally-expressed Dpp-GFP to induce ectopic BMP signaling.
source: Notably, in Pngl–/–; Mef2 > dpp GFP embryos, pMad staining was limited to PS3 and PS7, and ectopic pMad expression in the ectoderm was almost completely suppressed (Figure 6B and E), indicating that loss of Pngl dramatically decreases the ability of mesodermally-expressed Dpp-GFP to induce ectopic BMP signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the suppression of ectopic pMad in the ectoderm when Dpp-GFP is overexpressed in Pngl mutants.

claim: Mef2 > tkvCA embryos exhibit proper pMad staining in PS3 and PS7 in a Pngl+/+ background.
source: Mef2 > tkvCA embryos exhibited proper pMad staining in PS3 and PS7 in a Pngl+/+ background, although some pMad staining outside of PS7 could be seen in the VM marked by Fas3 (Figure 6G and G', arrows).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images in Figures 6G and G'.

claim: When tkvCA is overexpressed in Pngl mutant embryonic mesoderm, pMad is restored in PS3 and PS7.
source: When tkvCA is overexpressed in Pngl–/– embryonic mesoderm, pMad was restored in PS3 and PS7 and still some extra pMad positive cells were detected (Figure 6H and H', arrows).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images in Figures 6H and H'.

claim: About 30% of Pngl mutant animals with mesodermal tkvCA overexpression reach adulthood.
source: Moreover, ~30% of Pngl–/–; Mef2 > tkvCA animals reach adulthood (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is supported by eclosion test data in Figure 6I.

claim: Impaired BMP signaling is partially responsible for the lethality of Pngl mutant animals.
source: These observations further indicate that impaired BMP signaling is partially responsible for the lethality of Pngl–/– animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial rescue of lethality by tkvCA overexpression.

claim: The rescued Pngl mutant adults with mesodermal tkvCA overexpression do not show the acid zone loss and midgut shortening phenotypes observed in Pngl mutant adult escapers.
source: We note that the rescued Pngl–/–; Mef2 > tkvCA adults did not show the acid zone loss and midgut shortening phenotypes observed in Pngl–/– adult escapers (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic images in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The BMP-related midgut phenotypes of Pngl mutants persist to adulthood.
source: This indicates that the BMP-related midgut phenotypes of Pngl mutants persist to adulthood.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that rescued adults do not show midgut defects while escapers do.

claim: BMP signaling in visceral mesoderm requires an autoregulatory step to reach the required threshold for signaling to endoderm and this is the step during midgut development that is impaired in Pngl mutants.
source: Altogether, these results support the notion that BMP signaling in VM requires an autoregulatory step to reach the required threshold for signaling to endoderm and that this is the step during midgut development that is impaired in Pngl mutants.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments with Dpp-GFP and tkvCA.

claim: The developmental defect in BMP signaling contributes to the semi-lethality of Pngl mutants.
source: The data also indicate that this developmental defect contributes to the semi-lethality of Pngl mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial rescue of lethality by restoring BMP signaling.

claim: BMPs can function as homodimers or heterodimers to signal through homo- and/or heterodimeric type I receptors.
source: BMPs can function as homodimers or heterodimers to signal through homo- and/or heterodimeric type I receptors (Hogan, 1996; O'Connor et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Three BMP ligands have been identified in Drosophila: dpp, gbb, and scw.
source: To date, three BMP ligands have been identified in Drosophila: dpp, glass bottom boat (gbb) and screw (scw) (Arora et al., 1994; Doctor et al., 1992; Padgett et al., 1987; Wharton et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: scw is required in early embryogenesis, where it acts in combination with dpp to specify dorsal cell fates.
source: scw is required in early embryogenesis, where it acts in combination with dpp to specify dorsal cells fates (Arora et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: gbb and dpp mutants have both distinct and overlapping phenotypes during and after embryonic development.
source: gbb and dpp mutants have both distinct and overlapping phenotypes during and after embryonic development, suggesting that gbb and dpp are required together for proper signaling in some developmental contexts (Goold and Davis, 2007; Haerry et al., 1998; Hong et al., 2016; Khalsa et al., 1998; Wharton et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: gbb mutant embryos show reduced pMad staining in PS3.
source: Unlike control embryos (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1), gbbD4/D20 and gbbD4/D4 embryos showed reduced pMad staining in PS3 (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1), in agreement with previous work indicating that gastric caeca are somewhat short in gbb mutant larvae (Wharton et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1, and citation to published literature.

claim: In gbb mutant embryos, pMad staining in PS7 is increased and shifts anteriorly towards PS3.
source: However, in gbb–/– embryos pMad staining in PS7 is increased and shifts anteriorly towards PS3 (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In gbbD4/D20 embryos, the Dpp expression domain in PS7 is broader and stronger than controls and extends anteriorly to PS6.
source: However, the Dpp expression domain in PS7 is broader and stronger than controls in these embryos and extends anteriorly to PS6, and additional Dpp-positive puncta can be detected outside of the acid zone region towards PS3 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Dpp immunostaining images in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: At stage 16, gbb mutant embryos show an abnormal expansion of the second midgut compartment and a diffuse Labial staining both anteriorly and posteriorly to the second constriction.
source: At stage 16, gbb–/–embryos show an abnormal expansion of the second midgut compartment and a diffuse Labial staining both anteriorly and posteriorly to the second constriction (Figure 7D and D' and Figure 7—figure supplement 1) compared to controls (Figure 7B and B' and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images in Figures 7D and D' and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: gbb phenotypes in the midgut are quite different from dpp and Pngl loss-of-function phenotypes.
source: Therefore, gbb phenotypes in the midgut are quite different from dpp and Pngl loss-of-function phenotypes.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of phenotypes across different mutants.

claim: The strong and broader than normal pMad expression domain in gbb mutant PS7 indicates that BMP signaling in this region is mediated by Dpp homodimers alone.
source: The strong and broader than normal pMad expression domain in gbb–/– PS7 indicates that BMP signaling in this region is mediated by Dpp homodimers alone and Gbb likely limits the area in the VM wherein BMP autoactivation and signaling can occur.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that loss of Gbb results in increased BMP signaling in PS7.

claim: Gbb likely limits the area in the visceral mesoderm wherein BMP autoactivation and signaling can occur.
source: The strong and broader than normal pMad expression domain in gbb–/– PS7 indicates that BMP signaling in this region is mediated by Dpp homodimers alone and Gbb likely limits the area in the VM wherein BMP autoactivation and signaling can occur.
evidence: This is inferred from the expanded pMad domain in gbb mutants.

claim: Two type I receptors Tkv and Sax and one type II receptor (Punt) are involved in BMP signaling in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, two type I receptors Tkv and Saxophone (Sax) and one type II receptor (Punt) are involved in BMP signaling (Letsou et al., 1995; Nellen et al., 1994; Nellen et al., 1996; Ruberte et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mesodermal knockdown of tkv results in a severe reduction of pMad staining in PS7 and a partial loss of pMad in PS3.
source: As shown in Figure 6E, mesodermal knock-down of tkv results in a severe reduction of pMad staining in PS7 and a partial loss of pMad in PS3.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images in Figure 7E.

claim: The Dpp expression domain in PS7 fails to expand in Mef2 > tkvRNAi embryos.
source: Similar to Pngl–/– embryos, the Dpp expression domain in PS7 fails to expand in Mef2 > tkvRNAi embryos, although tkv KD does not seem to affect the intensity of Dpp staining at stage 13 or the presence of Dpp-positive puncta (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Dpp immunostaining images in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: In Mef2 > saxRNAi embryos, pMad staining in PS3 seems to be slightly decreased compared to controls, but it looks broader in PS7 and is extended anteriorly.
source: In Mef2 > saxRNAi embryos, pMad staining in PS3 seems to be slightly decreased compared to controls, but it looks broader in PS7 and is extended anteriorly (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images in Figure 7G.

claim: Mef2 > tkvRNAi embryos show a lack of second constriction and loss of Labial in the PS7 region.
source: Furthermore, Mef2 > tkvRNAi embryos show a lack of second constriction and loss of Labial in the PS7 region (Figure 7F and F').
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images in Figures 7F and F'.

claim: Mesodermal knockdown of sax does not show evident midgut constriction defects, but aberrant Labial staining is detectable both anteriorly and posteriorly to the second constriction.
source: In contrast, mesodermal knock-down of sax did not show evident midgut constriction defects, but aberrant Labial staining was detectable both anteriorly and posteriorly to the second constriction, similar to gbb–/– embryos (Figure 7H and H').
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images in Figures 7H and H'.

claim: BMP autoactivation in PS7 mesoderm is mediated by Dpp homodimers, as ligand, and Tkv homodimers, as receptor.
source: These results strongly suggest that BMP autoactivation in PS7 mesoderm is mediated by Dpp homodimers, as ligand, and Tkv homodimers, as receptor.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of gbb, sax, and tkv knockdown on BMP signaling in PS7.

claim: Dpp is synthesized as an inactive proprotein.
source: Similar to its vertebrate homologs, Dpp is synthetized as an inactive proprotein (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is supported by schematic in Figure 7I and knowledge of BMP processing.

claim: Following dimerization in the ER, Dpp proprotein dimers traffic through the secretory pathway, where they undergo cleavages to release the active dimer.
source: Following dimerization in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), Dpp proprotein dimers traffic through the secretory pathway, where they undergo cleavages to release the active dimer (Christian, 2012; Künnapuu et al., 2009; Sopory et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Control larvae exhibit two prominent bands on reducing gels: one corresponding to the full-length proprotein monomer and the other to the proprotein dimer.
source: When ran on a reducing gel, control larvae (y w and UAS-PnglRNAi without a GAL4 driver) exhibited two prominent bands: one corresponding in size to the full-length proprotein monomer and the other to the proprotein dimer, suggesting that Dpp dimers are partially resistant to the amount of reducing agents used in our assays (Figure 7J).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 7J.

claim: Dpp dimers are partially resistant to the amount of reducing agents used in the assays.
source: When ran on a reducing gel, control larvae (y w and UAS-PnglRNAi without a GAL4 driver) exhibited two prominent bands: one corresponding in size to the full-length proprotein monomer and the other to the proprotein dimer, suggesting that Dpp dimers are partially resistant to the amount of reducing agents used in our assays (Figure 7J).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of a dimer band on reducing gels.

claim: Larvae homozygous for Pngl alleles and those ubiquitously expressing Pngl dsRNA show an accumulation of a band corresponding to the prodomain and a significant decrease in the intensity of the band corresponding to Dpp dimers.
source: Larvae homozygous for Pngl alleles and those ubiquitously expressing Pngl dsRNA showed an accumulation of a band corresponding in size to the prodomain (cleavage product) and a significant decrease in the intensity of the band corresponding to Dpp dimers, without an apparent decrease in the intensity of the proprotein monomer band (Figure 7J).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 7J.

claim: Larvae heterozygous for the Pnglex14 allele display an intermediate pattern in the Western blot, suggesting that Pngl plays a dosage-sensitive role in Dpp dimerization and/or processing.
source: Of note, although larvae heterozygous for the Pnglex14 allele did not show any midgut defects (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), they displayed an intermediate pattern in the Western blot, suggesting that Pngl plays a dosage-sensitive role in Dpp dimerization and/or processing (Figure 7J).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 7J and inferred from the intermediate band pattern.

claim: Control larvae show two rather strong bands corresponding to Dpp dimers and a weaker band corresponding to a proprotein monomer on non-reducing gels.
source: Control larvae showed two rather strong bands corresponding in size to Dpp dimers and a weaker band corresponding to a proprotein monomer.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data on non-reducing gels.

claim: In a non-denaturing state, Dpp molecules are primarily found in association with other molecules and form Dpp-Dpp homodimers.
source: This indicates that in a non-denaturing state, Dpp molecules are primarily found in association with other molecules and form Dpp-Dpp homodimers.
evidence: This is inferred from the predominance of dimer bands on non-reducing gels.

claim: Pngl mutant and knockdown larvae show a significant decrease in Dpp dimers and a corresponding increase in the level of full-length monomer and cleavage product on non-reducing gels.
source: We found a significant decrease in Dpp dimers in Pngl mutant and knock-down larvae and a corresponding increase in the level of full-length monomer and the same cleavage product observed in regular Western blots.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data on non-reducing gels.

claim: Pngl is required for the formation and/or the stability of Dpp dimers.
source: In summary, these data provide strong evidence that Pngl is required for the formation and/or the stability of Dpp dimers.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing decreased Dpp dimers in Pngl mutants.

claim: Dpp dimers are not exclusively reduced in midguts of Pngl mutants but are also decreased in other parts of the larval body.
source: Dpp dimers are not exclusively reduced in midguts of Pngl mutants but are also decreased in other parts of the larval body (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Pngl regulates BMP signaling during embryonic midgut development without affecting BMP signaling in ectodermal and head regions of the embryo.
source: Here we report that fly Pngl regulates BMP signaling during embryonic midgut development without affecting BMP signaling in ectodermal and head regions of the embryo.
evidence: This is supported by pMad staining data showing tissue-specific effects.

claim: Pngl is not required in the midgut endoderm to receive the BMP signal, but rather is required in the visceral mesoderm to send the BMP signal.
source: Our data indicate that Pngl is not required in the midgut endoderm to receive the BMP signal, but rather is required in the VM to send the BMP signal.
evidence: This is supported by tissue-specific knockdown experiments.

claim: BMP signaling uses a paracrine/autocrine loop in the visceral mesoderm to sustain and increase the expression of Dpp in PS3 and PS7 of embryonic visceral mesoderm.
source: It has previously been shown that BMP signaling uses a paracrine/autocrine loop in the VM to sustain and increase the expression of Dpp in PS3 and PS7 of embryonic VM.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The BMP paracrine/autocrine loop ensures that the level of BMP ligands in the visceral mesoderm is high enough to induce signaling in the endoderm and to specify gastric caeca, the second midgut constriction and the acid zone.
source: This loop is proposed to ensure that the level of BMP ligands in the VM is high enough to induce signaling in the endoderm and to specify gastric caeca, the second midgut constriction and the acid zone (Bienz, 1997; Hursh et al., 1993; Staehling-Hampton and Hoffmann, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The BMP autoregulation mediated by the para-autocrine loop in the visceral mesoderm is the step which is impaired in Pngl-deficient embryos.
source: Several lines of evidence indicate that the BMP autoregulation mediated by the para-autocrine loop in the VM is the step which is impaired in Pngl-deficient embryos.
evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including dpp-lacZ and pMad staining.

claim: Loss of Pngl abolishes a BMP autoregulatory loop in the visceral mesoderm mediated by homodimers of Dpp acting through homodimers of Tkv.
source: Our data indicate that loss of Pngl abolishes a BMP autoregulatory loop in the VM mediated by homodimers of one ligand (Decapentaplegic; Dpp) acting through homodimers of one receptor (Thickveins; Tkv), and hence link a deglycosylation enzyme to tissue-specific regulation of BMP signaling in flies.
evidence: This is supported by genetic and biochemical data showing requirement for Dpp and Tkv homodimers.

claim: BMP heterodimers have stronger bioactivity than their homodimer counterparts.
source: In vitro and in vivo studies have shown that in general, BMP heterodimers have stronger bioactivity than their homodimers counterparts (Aono et al., 1995; Butler and Dodd, 2003; Israel et al., 1996; Little and Mullins, 2009; Morimoto et al., 2015; Valera et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Dpp has a higher affinity for Tkv, whereas Gbb and Scw have a higher affinity for Sax.
source: For example, in Drosophila, Dpp has a higher affinity for Tkv, whereas the other two ligands–Gbb and Scw–have a higher affinity for Sax (Bangi and Wharton, 2006b; O'Connor et al., 2006; Shimmi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Vertebrate and invertebrate BMP proteins and other members of the TGFβ superfamily each harbor several N-linked glycosylation sites.
source: Vertebrate and invertebrate BMP proteins and other members of the TGFβ superfamily each harbor several N-linked glycosylation sites, which have been shown to be glycosylated in many cases (Groppe et al., 1998; Miyazono and Heldin, 1989; Tauscher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: N-glycans on BMP ligands have various functional roles including enhancing receptor binding of BMP6, keeping TGFβ1 ligand in a latent state, and promoting inhibin heterodimer formation.
source: Various functional roles have been ascribed to N-glycans on these ligands, including enhancing receptor binding of BMP6 (Saremba et al., 2008), keeping the TGFβ1 ligand in a latent state (Miyazono and Heldin, 1989), and promoting inhibin (α/β) heterodimer formation at the expense of activin (β/β) homodimer formation (Antenos et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: It is possible that Pngl removes one or more N-glycans from Dpp and thereby promotes the formation or the stability of Dpp homodimers.
source: Accordingly, given the significant increase in Dpp monomeric forms and the simultaneous decrease in Dpp dimers upon loss of Pngl, it is possible that Pngl removes one or more N-glycans from Dpp and thereby promotes the formation or the stability of Dpp homodimers.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed effects on Dpp dimerization and known roles of N-glycans.

claim: Tissue-specific alterations in BMP signaling might contribute to some of the NGLY1 deficiency phenotypes including retinal abnormalities, delayed bone age and osteopenia, small feet and hands, and chronic constipation.
source: Given the reports on potential para-autocrine functions of mammalian Dpp homologs (Grimsrud et al., 1999; Rege et al., 2015; Shukunami et al., 2000; Tokola et al., 2015) and prominent human pathologies associated with dysregulated BMP signaling in ophthalmic, gastrointestinal and musculoskeletal systems (Wang et al., 2014), tissue-specific alterations in BMP signaling might contribute to some of the NGLY1 deficiency phenotypes including retinal abnormalities, delayed bone age and osteopenia, small feet and hands, and chronic constipation (Enns et al., 2014; Lam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings in Drosophila and known roles of BMP signaling in human disease.
